stages.title: Intermediate vocabulary
stages.hook: The words for book, library, author, story and number all share the letters ס־פ־ר. What do they have in common?
explain: Hebrew vocabulary grows from roots. The root ס־פ־ר (s-f-r) gives sefer (book), sifriya (library), sofer (author), sipur (story), mispar (number) and lesaper (to tell). The root idea is "counting and telling", and the pattern around it gives the exact meaning. Learn new words with their roots and you can guess others.

City words: beit kholim (hospital), universita (university), shuk (market), rofe (doctor), khaver (friend). Some words are borrowed from other languages, such as universita and telefon, and many everyday words come from Yiddish, Arabic and English.
From this level the words are written the way adults read them, with few niqqud, only where the reading would be unclear.
stages.mnemonic: S-f-r: counting and telling, from sefer to sipur.
sentences: The library is near the university.
My friend works in a hospital.
We eat at the restaurant today.

gq.q: Which word shares the root ס־פ־ר with sefer?
gq.why: Sipur comes from s-f-r. The others have other roots or are borrowed.

gq.q: What is a root in Hebrew?
o: A group of usually three letters that carries a core meaning
A kind of vowel mark that is written under letters
gq.why: Roots carry the core meaning, and patterns shape the exact word.

panel.q: A learner knows that "lehitkhaber" relates to khaver (friend). What can they guess?
o: The root kh-b-r is about connecting or friendship
The word means "to eat", from the same root
panel.why: Words from the same root share an idea.

panel.q: Why is it helpful to learn words with their roots?
o: One root gives several related words and helps guess new ones
Roots tell the plural form of every noun
panel.why: Related words share the root letters.

panel.q: Explain how the root s-f-r helps you understand sofer if you know sefer and sipur.
panel.model: They share the root s-f-r (books, telling, counting). The pattern -o-e- often names a person doing something, so sofer is a person who writes books, an author.
panel.why: Root plus pattern gives a predictable meaning.

teach.model: Most Hebrew words grow from a root of three letters. The root s-f-r gives sefer, sipur, sifriya and mispar. Knowing roots helps you guess new words.

stages.title: Verb forms and time expressions
stages.hook: "I wrote", "I write", "I will write": three times from one root. What changes?
explain: Hebrew verbs have a past, present and future. Past: katavti (I wrote). Present: kotev (I write, a man). Future: ekhtov (I will write), tikhtov (you will write), yikhtov (he will write). Future prefixes show the person: e-, ti-, yi-, ni-.

Verbs belong to patterns called binyanim. Pa'al is the simplest: katav. Pi'el often means intensive: limed (taught) from lamad (learned). Hif'il often means to cause: hikhtiv (dictated). Hitpa'el is reflexive: hitlabesh (got dressed).

Negation is simple: use lo before the verb for every tense: lo halakh (he did not go). For commands use al: al tizrok! (do not throw!). Time words: tamid (always), lif'amim (sometimes), akhshav (now), be-karov (soon), lifnei (before), akharei (after).
stages.mnemonic: Past: end changes. Future: front changes.

gq.q: Which prefix shows "he" in the future tense?
gq.why: Yi- is "he", ti- is "you" or "she", e- is "I", ni- is "we".

gq.q: What word negates a command, as in "do not throw"?
gq.why: Al + future form gives a prohibition.

panel.q: Why is "lo" enough to negate any tense in a statement?
o: Hebrew puts lo before the verb in every tense
Lo is only for the past
Lo is only for the past, and the present needs ein
panel.why: One negative word covers past, present and future.

panel.q: What does the binyan hitpa'el often express?
o: A reflexive action: doing something to oneself
Only the future, as in yikhtov

panel.q: Why do we say "lo halakh" for did not go, but "al telekh" for do not go?
panel.model: Lo negates statements; al is used for prohibitions, that is, negative commands.
panel.why: Hebrew separates ordinary negation from negative commands.

teach.model: Hebrew verbs have past, present and future forms. The future begins with e-, ti-, yi- or ni-. Negate with lo, and use al for a prohibition. Verbs belong to binyanim.

stages.title: Complex sentence introduction
stages.hook: "I stayed home because it rained." One small word joins the two ideas. In Hebrew it is only two letters long. Can you guess?
explain: Longer sentences are built with connectors: ki (because), aval (but), im (if), ke-she (when), akhar kakh (then), ad she- (until), le-khen (so), ve- (and). The word she- (that, which, who) is attached to the next word: ha-sefer she-karati, "the book that I read".

Unlike Arabic, Hebrew uses one form she- for who, which and that, for every gender and number. This is called a relative clause. Hebrew does not repeat the object pronoun with a direct object: ha-sefer she-karati, not "that I read it" (but with a preposition it does: ha-ish she-diberti ito, "the man I spoke with him").
Many small words are attached to the next word: ve-, be-, le-, ke-, she-, ha-. Learn to see them as separate parts of the written word.
stages.mnemonic: She- is a glue word: it sticks to the next word and links the clauses.
sentences: I stayed home because it rained.
The book that I read is long.
If you study well, you will succeed.

gq.q: What does the prefix she- mean?
gq.why: She- attaches to the following word to start a relative clause.

panel.q: Why is "ha-sefer she-karati" correct and not "ha-sefer she-karati oto"?
o: Hebrew does not repeat a direct object pronoun in such a clause
Oto is wrong in all sentences
Oto is wrong in all Hebrew sentences without exception
panel.why: Direct objects of the relative clause are usually not repeated.

panel.q: Which sentence is conditional?
o: im telekh, ani avo (if you go, I will come)
ani avo ki telekh (I will come because you go)

panel.q: Why do learners need to notice the attached letters ve-, be-, le-, she- and ha-?
panel.model: These small words are written attached to the next word, but each has its own meaning, so seeing them as separate parts helps you read and look words up.
panel.why: Hebrew writes many function words as prefixes.

teach.model: Use ki for because, aval for but and im for if. The prefix she- means who, which or that and starts a relative clause.

points.ask: How do I say the book that I read?

stages.title: Reading short stories
stages.hook: Many stories begin "Once upon a time". In Hebrew a story can start with "Hayo haya". What do you think that means?
explain: Stories often begin hayo haya, "once there was". Story parts in Hebrew: dmut (character), alila (plot), makom (setting), sof (end) and musar haskel (moral). A fairy tale usually has a king (melekh), a village (kfar) and a problem.

Modern Hebrew literature began to flourish after the language was revived as a spoken language in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Eliezer Ben-Yehuda championed this revival. Famous writers include the poet Haim Nahman Bialik, the novelist S. Y. Agnon (Nobel Prize 1966) and the writer Amos Oz.
When you read a story, look at the verbs first. Past tense often tells what happened. Find the characters, the place, the problem and the end (ha-sof).
sentences: Once there was a wise king.
The boy found a small key.
In the end the king laughed.

gq.q: Who is known for reviving Hebrew as a spoken language?
gq.why: Ben-Yehuda championed the revival of spoken Hebrew.

gq.q: Which Hebrew phrase is a common story opening?

panel.q: What is the "musar haskel"?
o: The moral or lesson of a story
The setting, which is the place of the story
panel.why: It is the lesson the story teaches.

panel.q: In "ha-yeled matsa maftéakh", what does the verb tell you?
o: The boy will find something tomorrow

panel.q: Name two things to look for when you read a short story.
panel.model: Look for the characters, the setting and the problem or plot, and how it ends.

teach.model: Many stories start with hayo haya, once there was. Look for characters, place, problem and ending. Modern Hebrew literature grew after the language was revived.

points.ask: What is special about Hebrew literature?

stages.title: Listening comprehension
stages.hook: The words "im" (with) and "im" (if) sound the same in Hebrew but are spelled differently. How can a listener tell them apart?
explain: In Modern Hebrew several letters share a sound. Most speakers say ח and כ the same (kh), ט and ת the same (t), כ and ק as k, and א and ע are both a very light glottal sound or silent. So words can sound alike: עִם (im, with) and אִם (im, if), or עֵת (et, time) and אֶת (et, the object marker).

Some communities, especially in the Mizrahi tradition, keep the difference between ח (a deeper h sound) and כ, or between ע and א. In ordinary news broadcasts you hear the common modern pronunciation.
When you listen, use context: the words before and after tell you which word was meant. Listen first for the topic, then for the key nouns and verbs, then for details.
stages.mnemonic: Same sound, different spelling: context is the detective.
sentences: Dew falls on the hill at night.

gq.q: Which two letters do most Hebrew speakers pronounce the same?
o: ב and מ, because both are lip sounds
gq.why: In modern speech both ח and כ (without dagesh) are kh.

gq.q: How can you tell "im" (with) from "im" (if) when you hear it?
o: From the context of the sentence
From the stress alone, which always differs

panel.q: Why can the words kol (all) and kol (voice) be confused when heard?
o: They sound exactly the same in modern Hebrew
They are spelled the same way in every book

panel.q: What does it suggest that some communities keep distinct ח and ע sounds?
o: Pronunciation traditions differ, and they preserve older distinctions
Everyone speaks exactly the same way in Israel
panel.why: Mizrahi and other traditions preserve older sounds.

panel.q: Give an example of two Hebrew words that sound the same but are spelled differently.
panel.model: Im (with) and im (if), or kol (all) and kol (voice).
panel.why: Modern Hebrew merges some letter sounds.

teach.model: In modern Hebrew some letters sound alike, like ח and כ. Words like im (with) and im (if) sound the same. Use context to decide.

points.ask: Do some words sound the same?
How do I tell them apart?

stages.title: Conversation and pronunciation
stages.hook: You need to interrupt politely, agree or ask for a moment. Which small Hebrew phrases make a conversation smooth?
explain: Conversation phrases: slikha (excuse me), betakh (sure), eyn be'ad ma (you are welcome), ani maskim (I agree), nidme li she- (it seems to me that), be-emet? (really?), ulai (maybe), rega (a moment).

Pronunciation hints: the r is usually uvular, the kh is rough, stress is mostly on the last part, and vowels are short and clear. Israelis speak quickly and drop some sounds in casual speech. Listen and repeat the rhythm.

Gender matters in conversation: a man says ani maskim, a woman says ani maskima; a man says ani batuakh (I am sure), a woman ani betukha. Use the form that fits the speaker or the person you are talking to.
stages.mnemonic: Slikha opens a door; rega buys a moment.
sentences: Excuse me, where is the station?
It seems to me that the idea is good.
Maybe we will meet at five.

gq.q: A woman says she agrees. Which form?
Which word asks someone to wait a moment?

panel.q: Why is "slikha" a good way to start a question to a stranger?
o: It is a greeting for friends only

panel.q: Which reply expresses doubt politely?
Give one way to disagree politely in Hebrew.
panel.model: You can say "ani lo maskim" (I do not agree) and soften it with "nidme li she-" or "aval".

teach.model: Use slikha to get attention, ani maskim to agree and ulai for maybe. Use nidme li she- to give an opinion. Remember the gender forms.

points.ask: How do I get someone's attention?
How do I agree or give an opinion?

stages.title: Writing paragraphs
stages.hook: A good paragraph guides the reader: first, next, finally. Which little words in Hebrew do that job?
explain: Paragraph linkers in Hebrew: kodem kol (first of all), shenit (second), akhar kakh (then), gam (also), aval (but), le-khen (therefore), lemashal (for example), le-sikum (in conclusion).
A paragraph has a main idea, supporting examples and a closing sentence. Keep the verb in the same tense, check that adjectives agree with nouns, and keep prefixes attached (ve-, ha-, be-).
Punctuation is like English: comma, full stop, question mark. Parentheses are reversed by the right-to-left direction. Abbreviations use a geresh (׳) or gershayim (״), as in ד״ר for doctor.
stages.mnemonic: First, then, finally: kodem kol, akhar kakh, le-sikum.
sentences: First of all I get up, and then I study.
I like summer but winter is cold.

gq.q: What does the geresh/gershayim in ד״ר show?
o: A question mark for a sentence
gq.why: Gershayim mark abbreviations before the final letter.

panel.q: Why do writers add "le-mashal"?
o: To introduce an example that supports the idea
To end the paragraph and sum up

panel.q: A student uses "ve-" before every sentence. How can they improve?
o: Use varied connectors like aval and le-khen
Remove all connectors and use only commas

panel.q: Name two features of a good paragraph.
panel.model: It has a clear main idea, supporting examples and a closing sentence.
panel.why: A paragraph is organised around one point.

teach.model: Begin with a main idea, add examples with le-mashal and link ideas with words like aval and le-khen. End with le-sikum.

points.ask: How do I support the idea?

stages.title: Cultural expressions and idioms
stages.hook: When someone has a birthday, Israelis say "mazal tov". What does the phrase literally mean?
explain: Hebrew has many fixed phrases. Mazal tov ("good luck") is said as "congratulations". Kol ha-kavod ("all the honour") means "well done". Be-te'avon means "enjoy your meal". Shana tova wishes a good year, and khag sameakh means "happy holiday".

Some phrases are shared with religious language but are used by everyone: toda la-El ("thank God"), im yirtse ha-Shem (God willing, mostly in religious circles). The saying kol hatkhala kasha, "every beginning is hard", is common advice for a learner.
Idioms are often picture-based: "lo nora" (not terrible) means "no problem"; "ein davar" means "never mind". Check the meaning in context, and notice that slang changes fast.
stages.mnemonic: Phrases are packages: open them for the meaning, not the words.
sentences: Happy holiday to you and your family.

gq.q: What do you say to a woman who is welcome?
gq.why: The feminine welcome is brukha ha-ba'a.

panel.q: Why would a literal translation of "mazal tov" as "good luck" mislead?
o: It is used to congratulate, not to wish luck before something
It is rude in Hebrew and is never used

panel.q: What does "kol hatkhala kasha" teach?
o: Starting something is the hardest part
Everything is hard, so do not start

panel.q: Why must idioms be learned as whole units?
panel.model: Their meaning is not found in the separate words, so a literal translation misleads. Learn the whole phrase and when to use it.

teach.model: Learn fixed phrases like mazal tov, kol ha-kavod and be-te'avon. Idioms have meanings that are not literal. Learn the whole phrase and its use.

points.ask: How do I understand an idiom?

stages.title: Practical travel communication
stages.hook: At Ben Gurion Airport, signs are in Hebrew, Arabic and English. Which Hebrew words would you like to know first?
explain: Travel words: sde te'ufa (airport), darkon (passport), kartis (ticket), malon (hotel), takhana (station), mapa (map), yamina (to the right), smola (to the left), yashar (straight). Ask politely: slikha, eifo ha-takhana?

A reservation is hazmana. A useful sentence is yesh li hazmana ba-malon, "I have a reservation at the hotel". For directions: pne yamina ve-akhar kakh hemshekh yashar, "turn right and then continue straight".

Good to know: in much of Israel, public transport does not run on Shabbat, from Friday afternoon to Saturday evening, so plan your trips. Signs are often in Hebrew, Arabic and English, and many people speak English.
stages.mnemonic: Yamina = right, smola = left; yashar = straight, like a ruler.
sentences: I have a reservation at the hotel.
Where can I buy a ticket?
Turn right and then continue straight.

o: To the left, as in smola
gq.why: Yamina = to the right; smola = to the left.

gq.q: Why might travellers in Israel check schedules around Shabbat?
o: Public transport mostly stops from Friday afternoon to Saturday evening
All shops are open and trains run as usual
It is a holiday for tourists only

panel.q: A sign says "takhanat rakevet". What is it?
o: An airport with a train line

panel.q: Why can a traveller manage with English in Israel, and still benefit from some Hebrew?
o: Many people speak English, but Hebrew helps with signs and warmth
English is not understood in Israel at all
Hebrew signs are always translated into every language
panel.why: A few words show respect and help in daily life.

panel.q: How would you ask politely where the station is?
panel.model: Slikha, eifo ha-takhana? (Excuse me, where is the station?)
panel.why: Polite opener plus eifo plus the place.

teach.model: Say slikha, then eifo and the place. Know the words for ticket, hotel, right and left. Public transport may stop on Shabbat.

points.ask: How do I ask where something is?
